items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of mitochondria.

rubric.why: Identifies the usual occurrence and location of centrioles.
rubric.how: Award for stating that centrioles are usually found in animal cells near the nucleus.

rubric.why: Describes the characteristic arrangement of the two centrioles.
rubric.how: Award for stating that centrioles occur as a pair arranged at right angles.

rubric.why: Gives the key structural detail of a centriole.
rubric.how: Award for stating that each centriole is a cylinder made of nine sets of three microtubules.

rubric.why: States the role of centrioles in cell division.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that centrioles help organize spindle fibres during cell division.

modelAnswer: Centrioles are small cylindrical structures found in the cytoplasm of animal cells, usually near the nucleus.
They occur as a pair, with the two centrioles arranged at right angles to each other; together they form the centrosome.
Each centriole consists of nine sets of three microtubules arranged in a cylinder.
During cell division, centrioles help organize the spindle fibres that move chromosomes.

items.followUp: Explain why scientific names are useful in identifying organisms.

rubric.why: Explains the two-part basis of a binomial name.
rubric.how: Award for stating that each organism has a two-part scientific name consisting of its genus and species.

rubric.why: Recognizes that scientific names are used internationally.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that scientists throughout the world use the same universal name for an organism.

rubric.why: States how binomial nomenclature avoids ambiguity in common names.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it avoids confusion caused by different common names in different places.

rubric.why: Explains the value of a standardized naming system for identification and communication.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that standardized scientific names help identify organisms and allow accurate communication.

modelAnswer: In binomial nomenclature, each organism is given a two-part scientific name: the first part is its genus and the second is its species.
The system provides a universal name used by scientists throughout the world.
It avoids confusion because one organism may have different common names in different places.
Standardized scientific names make organisms easier to identify and allow accurate communication among biologists.

items.followUp: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration with respect to oxygen, products and energy yield.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the processes by whether oxygen is used.
rubric.how: Award for stating that aerobic respiration requires oxygen and anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen.

rubric.why: Compares how fully glucose is broken down.
rubric.how: Award for distinguishing complete breakdown in aerobic respiration from incomplete breakdown in anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies the end products of aerobic respiration and an accepted form of anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award for giving carbon dioxide and water as aerobic products and lactic acid or ethanol as an anaerobic product.

rubric.why: Compares the energy yield stated in the answer.
rubric.how: Award for giving about 36 ATP for aerobic respiration and 2 ATP for anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Rewards a correct overall reaction summary for either process.
rubric.how: Award for writing a correct word equation or reaction summary for aerobic respiration or either common form of anaerobic respiration.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen and completely breaks down glucose: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (about 36 ATP).
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and incompletely breaks down glucose.
In muscles, glucose → lactic acid + energy (2 ATP); in yeast, glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy (2 ATP).
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration.

items.followUp: Differentiate between the cell wall and the plasma membrane.

rubric.why: Describes when the primary wall forms and its properties.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the primary wall forms first and is thin and flexible, allowing the cell to grow.

rubric.why: Describes when and where the secondary wall forms and its properties.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the secondary wall is deposited inside the primary wall after growth stops and is generally thicker and more rigid.

modelAnswer: The primary wall is formed first and is thin and flexible, allowing the cell to grow.
The secondary wall is deposited on the inner side of the primary wall after the cell stops growing; it is usually thicker and more rigid.
